flawed_step: Lines 46–64 claim every cyclic directed graph has multiple transitive reductions. The construction does not apply to a cycle of length 2.
counterexample: Let G have vertices {a,b} and edges a→b and b→a. G is cyclic. Its transitive closure contains reachability in both directions (and self-reachability through the cycle, if positive-length paths are used). Any graph with this closure must contain at least two edges. With two vertices, achieving both a→b and b→a using only two edges uniquely requires exactly {a→b,b→a}; self-loops cannot replace either cross-edge. Thus G has a unique transitive reduction despite being cyclic.
assessment_summary: The claimed equivalence is false for a directed 2-cycle. In particular, the alternative Hamiltonian-cycle construction at line 53 requires v3 and therefore cannot handle k=2.
